preamble: Dissibilation of the voiced dental/alveolar affricate [dz] to the voiced non-sibilant dental fricative [ð]: the stop closure is lost and the sibilant groove flattens, leaving a weak dental fricative. It is reconstructed for two unrelated developments. In Albanian, the Proto-Albanian reflex of the Proto-Indo-European palatovelars *ǵ and *ǵʰ is commonly set up as *dz, which became dh /ð/ (dhëmb 'tooth'). In Castilian Spanish, Mackenzie (2022), following Menéndez Pidal's description of a 16th-century voiced interdental ẓ, argues that Old Spanish /dz/ (written z, as in hazer, dezir) had dissibilated to /ð/ by the early 1500s before merging with /θ/; the standard account instead posits deaffrication to [z̪] and devoicing before any interdental stage.

examples.note: Reconstructed stage: the palatal series *ǵ, *ǵʰ gives *dz > *ð > dh, parallel to *ḱ > *ts > *θ > th (EPA *tserā > thjerë 'lentil'). Some scholars (e.g. Matzinger) reconstruct the pre-Albanian stage as *j́ or *ð without an affricate.
The *dz reconstruction is Orel's; Demiraj and Matzinger give different Proto-Albanian forms. Cognate with Latin gener, Ancient Greek gambrós.

examples.from: Old Spanish hazer [aˈdzeɾ] 'to do, make' (< Latin facere)
examples.note: Stage reconstructed by Mackenzie (2022) from late medieval spelling of d as z in preconsonantal coda position (where /d/ was [ð]); Menéndez Pidal describes the interdental pronunciation θ and ẓ (= /ð/) as becoming general in the 16th century, citing plaça, hazer.

examples.from: Old Spanish dezir [deˈdziɾ] 'to say' (< Latin dīcere)
examples.note: Same development of intervocalic z; the voiced /ð/ then merged with voiceless /θ/ (the reflex of ç /ts/) shortly afterwards.

sources: Mackenzie, I. (2022). The Genesis of Spanish /θ/: A Revised Model. Languages 7(3), 191. https://doi.org/10.3390/languages7030191
